evals.name: concurrent-transactions
evals.prompt: I want to actually understand how databases handle concurrent transactions. I keep reading about isolation levels — read committed, repeatable read, snapshot isolation, serializable — but it never sticks. I can't explain the differences a week later, even though I work with Postgres every day. I'm a backend engineer, comfortable writing SQL but I've never built a database engine. Help me really learn this — I want to come away able to explain it cleanly and still remember it next month. I have about an hour today and 20 min/day after that.
evals.expected_output: A goal-clarifying response (or confirming defaults), a Feynman-style or first-principles explanation that starts with what isolation actually IS rather than just listing the levels, an active-recall component (asks the user to explain or apply something), durable artifacts saved to disk including a markdown summary/cheat sheet AND flashcards (HTML or Anki TSV) AND a spaced-repetition schedule, and a clear next step for the user.
expectations: Response quickly establishes or assumes a learning goal (understand-it / use-it / pass-it / etc.) rather than diving into a wall of text
Response uses an active-recall, Feynman, or first-principles framing — does not just lecture passively
Response asks the user to produce something (explain in own words, predict, or answer a question) AND signals that it is waiting for the user, rather than asking and immediately self-answering
Response saves a markdown notes/cheat-sheet file with concrete useful content on isolation levels (mentions at least three of: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read, lost update, write skew)
Response generates flashcards or an Anki deck or an HTML flashcard app file with at least 5 cards covering the topic
Response generates a spaced-repetition schedule (markdown or .ics file or both) targeting the topic
Response calls out the right reference scripts/files (e.g. uses generate_flashcards_html.py / generate_schedule.py / generate_anki_deck.py from the skill)
Response explicitly tells the user when/how to come back for the next session

evals.name: raft-interview-prep
evals.prompt: I have a software architecture interview at a fintech next Tuesday and they told me to be ready on distributed consensus — specifically Raft. I get the high-level idea (leader, log replication, voting) but I always freeze when I'm asked to walk through edge cases — network partitions, leader failures during log replication, what happens to in-flight commits, how log compaction works. I'm a senior backend engineer, 8 years in, but I've never operated a Raft system in production. I have maybe 6 hours total to prep over the next 5 days. Help me get sharp.
evals.expected_output: Recognition that this is exam/interview prep with a clear deadline, a brief diagnostic that probes the user's stated weak spots (network partitions, leader failures, etc.) rather than retreating to safer basics, a 5-day plan that fits ~6 hours total, generation of a quiz HTML file with scenario-based questions, and explicit running of an active-recall session on the user's weak spots.
expectations: Response identifies the goal as exam/interview prep (pass-it framing) with a 5-day deadline rather than treating it as open-ended understanding
Response includes diagnostic questions that target the user's stated weak spots (network partitions, leader failures, log replication edge cases) — not just basic 'what is Raft' questions
Response includes scenario-based questions or stress-tests rather than only conceptual questions
Response saves a quiz HTML file (using generate_quiz_html.py) or equivalent quiz artifact with at least 5 scenario questions
Response saves a markdown study plan/cheat sheet covering the topics mentioned (leader election, log replication, partition handling, log compaction)
Response produces a time-budgeted plan that fits 6 hours over 5 days (does not propose a 40-hour curriculum)
Response asks the user to do something active right now — answer a diagnostic question, explain something — rather than only delivering a plan
Response signals it is waiting for the user's input rather than answering its own questions

evals.name: mandarin-memorization
evals.prompt: I'm teaching myself basic Mandarin Chinese and I'm trying to memorize the 100 most common characters so I can recognize them in context. I just keep forgetting them between sessions. I have about 30 minutes a day, every day, for as long as it takes. I'd love a real system — not just a list to stare at. Help me make this stick.
evals.expected_output: A memorization-focused approach (not 'understand it'), generation of an Anki TSV deck or HTML flashcards covering at least 20 high-frequency characters (with character / pinyin / meaning), a spaced-repetition schedule using the skill's generate_schedule.py, encoding tips beyond rote (mnemonics, radicals, chunking), and a daily 30-min protocol the user can follow.
expectations: Response treats this as a remember-it / memorization goal, not a conceptual-understanding goal
Response generates an Anki deck (TSV) or HTML flashcards file with at least 20 actual cards (not just placeholder text), each containing the character, pinyin, and meaning at minimum
Response generates a spaced-repetition schedule (markdown and/or .ics)
Response provides memory-encoding strategies beyond rote review (radicals, mnemonics, chunking by category, or similar) — not just 'review the list'
Response provides a concrete daily 30-min protocol the user can follow (e.g. structured into review + new material + recall test)
Response either uses the actual generation scripts (generate_anki_deck.py, generate_flashcards_html.py, generate_schedule.py) or creates equivalent artifacts manually
Response acknowledges the user has indefinite time horizon (rather than imposing an artificial deadline)

evals.name: rust-cli-roadmap
evals.prompt: I want to learn enough Rust over the next 8 weeks to ship a small CLI tool I've been wanting to build — a markdown linter for my company's docs style guide. I have about 5 hours per week. I have a lot of Python and TypeScript experience (12 years), but Rust ownership has stumped me twice when I've tried it before — I bounced off it both times. Make me a real plan, and let's get started today.
evals.expected_output: An 8-week roadmap with stages, checkpoints, and concrete resources, recognition that ownership is a known weak spot (and addressing it head-on early), a deliberate-practice element rather than just reading lists, the user being asked to start today (not 'when ready'), and artifacts saved to disk (the roadmap markdown at minimum, ideally also a spaced-repetition schedule for ownership concepts).
expectations: Response produces an 8-week roadmap in markdown form with clear stages and checkpoints (not just 'study this for a while, then move on')
Response calibrates the plan to ~5 hours/week (40 hours total), not a 100-hour fantasy plan
Response treats ownership as a specifically-flagged weak point and addresses it with deliberate practice early (not 'read chapter 4 and you'll be fine')
Response includes specific named resources (books, courses, doc sections, exercises like Rustlings or Exercism) — not just 'find a Rust tutorial'
Response ties checkpoints to concrete artifacts (working code, exercises completed, etc.) rather than 'feel comfortable with X'
Response saves the roadmap to a markdown file on disk
Response starts the first session today rather than only handing over a plan
Response asks the user to engage actively (a starting question, an exercise, or running through a concept) rather than ending with 'good luck'
